nameStory: This climbing beauty gets its name from the dramatic dark purple-black center, or 'eye,' that contrasts strikingly with its bright orange, yellow, or white petals. The name connects to old folk ballads about a character called Black-eyed Susan, though this African native shares the common name with our familiar native wildflowers in the daisy family.
description: Black-eyed Susan vine is a fast-growing climbing plant from East Africa that's popular in New England gardens and hanging baskets. This herbaceous perennial produces cheerful trumpet-shaped flowers with distinctive dark centers throughout the growing season. The vine can climb 6-8 feet in a season, twining around supports with its flexible stems and heart-shaped leaves.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Distinctive trumpet-shaped blooms about 1-2 inches across with five flat, rounded petals (usually orange or yellow) surrounding a deep purple-black throat that feels velvety to touch

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped leaves with pointed tips, arranged opposite each other on the stem, feeling soft and slightly fuzzy with visible veins

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Twining vine that climbs by wrapping its flexible green stems around supports, growing rapidly upward or cascading from containers

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Round, beaked seed capsules that make a rattling sound when dry and mature, splitting open to release dark seeds

habitat: Found exclusively in cultivated settings throughout New England - gardens, patios, and porches where it's grown in containers or trained up trellises and arbors. This tender tropical plant cannot survive New England winters outdoors and doesn't escape cultivation to become established in wild areas.

seasonality.spring: Seeds are planted indoors in late winter or outdoors after last frost. Young plants emerge with small heart-shaped leaves and begin their climbing growth.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with continuous flowers from early summer through fall. Vines reach full size and cover supports with dense foliage.
seasonality.fall: Continues flowering until first frost, when the entire plant dies back. Seed pods mature and can be collected for next year's planting.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground presence in New England - this tropical plant cannot survive freezing temperatures and must be replanted each year.

funFact: Despite being called 'Black-eyed Susan vine,' this African climber is completely unrelated to our native Black-eyed Susan wildflowers - they're not even in the same plant family, proving that common names can be wonderfully confusing!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with native Rudbeckia species (the 'real' Black-eyed Susans), but those are upright wildflowers with daisy-like blooms, not climbing vines with trumpet flowers. Remember: if it climbs and has trumpet flowers, it's the vine; if it stands upright with daisy flowers, it's the wildflower.
contextualKnowledge: The shared 'Black-eyed Susan' name creates endless confusion since the vine and the native wildflowers (Rudbeckia species) are completely unrelated plants from different continents and plant families. Both simply happen to have dark centers that reminded people of the same folk song character.
compareHints: This is the only Thunbergia species commonly grown in New England gardens. Among other climbing vines with trumpet flowers, morning glories have larger, more funnel-shaped blooms without the distinctive dark throat, while trumpet vine has much larger orange flowers and compound leaves rather than simple heart-shaped ones.
